title: Meal Delivery Unit Economics
takeaway: Check contribution on one unit before buying more demand.

title: Profit vs Cash: A Working Capital Crunch
takeaway: Match invoice timing to the cash you must fund before collection.

title: Revenue Growth vs Operating Expenses
takeaway: Bridge the change in profit rather than blaming the largest revenue line.

title: SaaS CAC Payback vs Cash Runway
takeaway: Profitable customer lifetime value does not fund today's acquisition bill.

title: Inventory and the Cash Conversion Cycle
takeaway: Treat days between supplier payment and collection as a financing requirement.

title: Membership Business Break-Even
takeaway: Prove the current unit's economics before copying its fixed costs.

title: Price Discounts and Gross Profit
takeaway: Calculate the profit given away, not just the percentage cut in price.

title: Gross Margin vs a Volume Discount
takeaway: Require evidence for the additional volume needed to preserve contribution.

title: Special-Order Pricing on Idle Capacity
takeaway: Separate incremental contribution from allocated costs that stay either way.

title: Enterprise Pricing and Hidden Cost to Serve
takeaway: Include the scarce support work that a shared overhead pool conceals.

title: Price Objections: Read the Lost-Deal Evidence
takeaway: Validate the buying obstacle before spending margin on a concession.
work: 31 ÷ 40 = 77.5% of reviewed lost deals went to a competitor within 5% of the quote.
Only 9 reviewed losses fall outside that observed price band; this does not by itself establish causality.
Pair the price evidence with the stated response-time and scope complaints before changing the offer.

title: Promotions and Full-Price Demand
takeaway: Measure whether a promotion creates demand or moves purchases into a cheaper window.
work: Full-price sell-through is down 30%, so an illustrative prior index of 100 is now 70.
There have been five consecutive predictable end-of-month promotions.
Compare full-month contribution and purchase timing; the prompt does not provide enough margin data to compute the net profit effect.

title: Warehouse Capacity: Orders and Shipments
takeaway: Increase finished shipments at the binding step, not input to an overloaded queue.
work: Incoming orders = 340/day; shipping capacity = 200/day.
Daily backlog increase = 340 − 200 = 140 orders.
Even unlimited additional demand cannot raise shipments above 200/day without fulfillment relief.

title: Roastery Capacity Across Sequential Steps
takeaway: The lowest practical capacity sets output in a serial process.
work: Roasting rate = 400 ÷ 8 = 50 lb/hour.
Serial output ceiling = min(400 roasting, 700 packaging, 520 demand) = 400 lb/day.
Demand exceeds roasting output by 520 − 400 = 120 lb/day, equivalent to 2.4 extra roasting hours at the stated rate.

title: Freight Bookings, Coverage and Delivery
takeaway: Follow each stage of the operating funnel to locate the widening gap.
work: Uncovered loads last month = 310 − 305 = 5; this month = 425 − 342 = 83.
The booking-to-coverage gap widened by 78 loads; investigate carrier sourcing before buying more leads.

title: Machine Upgrades and Line Throughput
takeaway: A faster non-constraint can create inventory without creating output.
work: Station cycle times are 40, 95 and 55 seconds per unit.
The 95-second assembly step caps ideal serial throughput at 3,600 ÷ 95 ≈ 37.9 units/hour.
Changing cutting from 40 to 20 seconds leaves the 95-second maximum unchanged.

title: Job Mix and Shifting Bottlenecks
takeaway: Compare contribution released per constrained hour across job types.
work: Two job types each account for roughly half of revenue, but revenue share is not contribution per hour.
For each constraint, calculate incremental contribution unlocked ÷ additional constrained hours.
The prompt does not provide those margins or hours, so it does not support a numerical winner; gather them before choosing.

title: Manufacturing Scrap Rate Step Change
takeaway: Investigate a dated quality change before adding capacity to absorb defects.
work: Week 1 scrap rate = 60 ÷ 2,000 = 3%.
Starts rose only 5% from week 1 to week 4 while passing units fell by 250; trace the change around week 3.

title: Unanswered Sales Calls vs More Ad Spend
takeaway: Recover demand you already paid for before purchasing more of it.
work: Unanswered calls = 900 × 40% = 360/month.
Answered calls = 900 − 360 = 540/month.
Recover the existing 360 missed opportunities before buying another batch; the prompt does not state their close rate.

title: Sales Appointments and Unused Capacity
takeaway: Match the intervention to appointment supply before adding salespeople.
work: Appointment utilization = 7 ÷ 20 = 35%.
Unfilled appointment capacity = 20 − 7 = 13 per salesperson per week.
At the stated close rate, additional qualified appointments could use existing sales capacity; verify lead quality rather than assuming every slot will fill.

title: E-Commerce Conversion vs Paid Traffic
takeaway: Separate conversion economics from traffic volume before increasing spend.
work: Current orders = 60,000 × 0.4% = 240/month.
Traffic cost = 60,000 × $0.90 = $54,000/month.
At 0.8% conversion, the same traffic would yield 480 orders; that is a scenario to test, not a guaranteed lift.

title: Sales Funnel vs Delivery Capacity
takeaway: A booking is not a delivered job; inspect the full commercial-to-delivery chain.
work: Sales rose from 72 to 94, a gain of 22; completed jobs fell from 70 to 61, a drop of 9.
This month's sales minus completions = 94 − 61 = 33 jobs, versus 2 last month.
Investigate production and capacity before adding more demand to the delivery queue.

title: Customer Acquisition vs Churn
takeaway: Reconcile gross additions with net growth before funding another acquisition push.
work: Net growth = new customers − lost customers.
Implied departures = 1,200 − 150 = 1,050 customers, assuming no other customer-count movements.
Only 150 of 1,200 gross additions remain as net growth while acquisition cost is up 12%; diagnose retention first.

title: Rising CAC and Channel Saturation
takeaway: Test concentration and audience limits instead of assuming every CAC rise is creative fatigue.
work: A 60% CAC increase turns an illustrative prior CAC of 100 cost units into 160.
With 80% of growth tied to this channel, a cost shock is concentrated rather than diversified.
Unchanged conversion weakens a conversion-failure explanation; test audience saturation and alternatives before a large creative commitment.

title: Competing with a National Chain on Price
takeaway: Choose a dimension where your capabilities can earn a return.
work: A competitor priced 25% below a hypothetical $100 title would charge $75.
Matching that gap requires removing $25 from your price; your buying cost is not given, so no profitable matching price can be inferred.
Compare differentiated service and customer value instead of assuming equal purchasing economics.

title: SaaS Segment Retention and Focus
takeaway: Compare retention and service burden before spreading a small team across segments.
work: Dentist renewal is 91%, versus about 55% in the other segments: a 36-percentage-point gap.
Per illustrative 100 renewal opportunities, that is 91 retained versus 55; do not confuse this with an acquisition forecast.
Dentists are currently 15% of customers; combine retention, referrals and support burden when allocating the next effort.

title: Local Density vs New-City Expansion
takeaway: Price the new operating system a distant market requires.
work: Both options add three stores; the current network has six profitable stores.
The existing metro already supports 9% same-store sales growth; this is evidence of current traction, not a guarantee for new sites.
A city 200 miles away adds supply and management requirements not quantified in the prompt; include them before treating the options as equal.

title: Warehouse Build vs Outsource
takeaway: Stress-test fixed commitments against the demand floor, not just the average.
work: At 40,000 orders, the stated per-order difference is $6.40 − $4.10 = $2.30, or $92,000/month once full efficiency is reached.
A simple $1.9M ÷ $92,000 ≈ 20.7-month payback ignores the ramp and assumes the stated costs remain valid.
Volume has ranged from 22,000 to 55,000 and efficiency takes a year; test the low-volume fixed-cost case rather than relying on that simple average.

title: Sunk Cost vs the Next Product Investment
takeaway: Allocate the next dollar using future alternatives, not unrecoverable past spending.
work: The $1.8M already spent cannot be recovered by either next decision.
The live alternatives use the same next $900,000; the core is expected to return about $2.5M.
$2.5M ÷ $900,000 ≈ 2.78, based on an estimate rather than a guaranteed return; compare forward opportunities, not past cost.

title: A Bounded Experiment Before Market Entry
takeaway: Spend to resolve a decision-changing uncertainty before making a large commitment.
work: Full entry commits $4M and a dedicated team.
The $12M projection is a three-year forecast, not observed demand; no target buyers have been contacted.
Define a smaller test budget and evidence gate before choosing whether the full $4M commitment is justified.

title: Hiring Payback: Billable Time vs Assistant Cost
takeaway: Released owner time has economic value only when it can be used.
work: Potential billable value of six hours = 6 × $250 = $1,500/week.
Assistant cost for six hours = 6 × $22 = $132/week.
Difference before additional employer costs and ramp = $1,368/week, conditional on converting those freed hours into paid client work.

title: New-Hire Onboarding Ownership
takeaway: Give the ramp one accountable owner and an observable learning plan.
work: Three days have passed without a named trainer or plan.
There is no wage, output or ramp-rate data, so the prompt does not support a dollar payback calculation.
Assign an owner, define first-week tasks and check demonstrated capability before adding more unstructured shadowing.

title: Key-Person Dependency in Production
takeaway: Convert individual knowledge into a repeatable process and trained backup.
work: One knowledge holder and zero trained backups means absence can stop the entire process.
Two years without leave does not quantify outage probability, but the prompt confirms production stops when that person is out.
Document the recipes and validate a second baker's ability to run them; a retention payment alone does not create backup capacity.

title: Delegating Decisions vs Checklists
takeaway: Move decision authority with responsibility rather than retaining every exception.
work: A 14-step checklist still produces about 12 escalations a day.
The checklist describes actions but does not allocate authority for exceptions.
Define outcome, boundaries and escalation triggers, then measure whether routine decisions stay with the supervisor.

title: Hiring Lead Time and Productive Capacity
takeaway: Plan hiring from the date useful capacity is needed, accounting for ramp.
work: Recruiting takes eight weeks, roughly two months.
Productivity ramp takes another three months: total lead time is about five months.
Current utilization is 100% and demand is contracted for two quarters, so compare that five-month delay with capacity needed now.

title: Sales Incentives and Customer Trust
takeaway: Pair an incentive with guardrails for the value it might consume.
work: Revenue per repair order rose 22%, but repeat visits fell 15%.
The rating declined by 4.5 − 3.8 = 0.7 points and unnecessary-work complaints doubled.
The prompt does not quantify lifetime revenue loss; the conflicting indicators justify an incentive review, not a claim that short-term revenue proves success.

title: Allocating a Scarce Asset
takeaway: Compare the incremental value of the next constrained unit of capacity.

title: Customer Acquisition Cost Across Channels
takeaway: Use the marginal acquisition opportunity rather than the size of a budget.

title: Marketing Budget and Diminishing Returns
takeaway: Compare the next dollar's return after the best opportunities are already funded.

title: Contribution per Constrained Machine Hour
takeaway: Rank jobs by the return on the resource they actually compete for.

title: Allocating Senior Engineer Time
takeaway: Include the scarce specialist attention each project consumes.

title: Truck Purchase vs Variable Carrier Costs
takeaway: Value reversibility when the demand supporting a fixed investment is uncertain.
work: Buying two trucks commits $260,000 to obtain a stated 20% per-load saving.
About 60% of recent growth depends on one contract rebidding in seven months.
Load counts and cost per load are absent, so payback cannot be calculated; compare flexible coverage with the risk of stranded fixed capacity.

title: Checkout Outage and Incident Prioritization
takeaway: Triage by blocked business outcomes and blast radius, not request volume.
work: The cosmetic issue affects 3% of users; the checkout issue blocks payment for 100% of new signups.
The affected populations differ, so do not infer a precise revenue ratio from those percentages.
Restore the blocked acquisition/payment path first; separately schedule the reporting and cosmetic work.

title: Declining Reviews and Future Demand Risk
takeaway: Separate a compounding operating problem from a static inconvenience.
work: The rating fell by 4.6 − 4.1 = 0.5 points over two months.
The vendor increase is 8%; the booking flow has six clicks, but no conversion losses are supplied.
A deteriorating reputation can affect future bookings repeatedly; investigate its cause without inventing an exact cash impact.

title: Expansion with a Single Trainer
takeaway: Resolve a critical dependency before copying it across new locations.
work: Four new locations are planned on top of three existing ones.
Only one manager can train staff; adding sites does not add trainer capacity.
Standardize the process and validate another trainer before replicating the same dependency across four openings.

title: An Irreversible Lease Commitment
takeaway: Spend deliberation time in proportion to the cost of reversing a decision.
work: The lease fixes a commitment over five years; the other decisions can be changed more readily.
Lease payments and exit terms are not supplied, so the total financial commitment cannot be computed.
Compare reversibility and downside across plausible futures; devote deliberation to the harder-to-reverse choice.

title: Supplier Concentration and Outage Risk
takeaway: Recalculate the downside when the backup capacity disappears.
work: The proposed material saving is about $340,000/year, or 7%.
The prior two-week outage cost about $200,000 when this supplier provided 45% of input and alternatives still existed.
Consolidation changes the outage exposure; neither the new loss nor outage probability is supplied, so do not treat $200,000 as the new risk estimate.

title: Customer Concentration and Renewal Risk
takeaway: Build alternatives while a concentrated relationship is healthy.
work: One customer provides 70% of revenue; all others together provide 30%.
Losing that customer would leave 30% of today's revenue before replacement or other changes.
A happy customer is not a renewal guarantee; develop alternatives before an annual renewal becomes a crisis.
